subject: Behavioral Economics
title: Optimism Bias in Borrowing
description: Learn Optimism Bias in Borrowing in one minute.

hook.text: 'I'll pay it off next month.' Every credit card holder has said it. Most don't.

buildup.text: Optimism bias: we believe our future self will earn more, spend less, and be more disciplined. Evidence says otherwise.

discovery.text: Bar-Gill found that consumers methodically underestimate how long they'll carry credit card balances by an average.

twist.text: Lenders profit from this. They offer low teaser rates knowing most borrowers will carry balances well past.

climax.text: Assume your future self won't change. If you can't repay it this month, don't borrow it.

punchline.text: Your future self isn't more responsible. Plan accordingly.

quiz.question: How does optimism bias affect borrowing?
options: People borrow less than they need
People overestimate their ability to repay, carrying balances longer

details.summary: Optimism bias leads borrowers to overestimate their future income, underestimate repayment difficulty, and believe they will pay off debt faster than they actually do. This systematically leads people to take on more debt than they can comfortably handle.
details.whyItMatters: Optimism bias in borrowing contributed to the 2008 mortgage crisis and continues to drive credit card and student loan over-indebtedness. Borrowers consistently plan based on best-case scenarios rather than realistic ones.
takeaways: Borrowers systematically overestimate future ability to repay
Optimism bias leads to taking on debt that is unmanageable under realistic scenarios
Cooling-off periods and realistic repayment calculators reduce overborrowing

faq.question: How does optimism bias lead to excessive borrowing?
faq.answer: People imagine future scenarios where they earn more, spend less, and face no unexpected expenses. They plan repayment based on this optimistic projection rather than realistic or pessimistic ones, leading to borrowing amounts that only work under ideal conditions.

faq.question: Why did optimism bias contribute to the mortgage crisis?
faq.answer: Both borrowers and lenders assumed home prices would keep rising and incomes would increase. Adjustable-rate mortgages were taken with the optimistic belief that refinancing or income growth would handle higher payments. Reality fell far short.
